key_results: The signals-and-systems abstraction characterizes a physical, mathematical, or computational object solely by how it maps an input signal to an output. Because the representation suppresses substrate details, the same form is widely applicable, modular, and hierarchical. [Session 1, slides 7–14]

Sampling forms a DT sequence x[n]=x(nT) from a CT signal; reconstruction maps samples back to CT, with zero-order hold and piecewise-linear interpolation presented as two distinct practical rules. [Session 1, slides 15–18]

For the linear leaky tank, conservation plus outflow proportional to height gives dr1/dt=(r0−r1)/τ. The constant τ has units of time and determines the exponential approach to steady state. [Session 1, slides 25–35]

DT systems are deliberately represented four ways: a verbal rationale, a compact difference equation, a signal-flow block diagram, and an operator expression. Equations state constraints, while block diagrams also specify an executable signal-flow interpretation and input/output roles. [Session 2, slides 3–21]

With R denoting one unit of right shift, a DT realization made from adders, gains, and delays can be manipulated as a polynomial or rational expression in R. Cascades multiply operator expressions, and distributive/associative/commutative algebra reveals equivalent realizations when systems start at rest. [Session 2, slides 22–35]

The accumulator obeys (1−R)Y=X and has functional 1/(1−R)=1+R+R²+…, so a one-sample transient produces a persistent unit-step response. Feedback appears as a cyclic signal path, and each traversal adds another output sample. [Session 2, slides 36–47]

An acyclic finite add/gain/delay network has a finite-duration impulse response, whereas a cyclic network can have an infinite-duration response. A single loop of gain p produces the fundamental mode p^n u[n], converging for |p|<1 and diverging for |p|>1. [Session 2, slides 43–56; Session 3, slides 5–12]

Higher-order rational DT systems factor into first-order pole factors. Partial fractions rewrite their impulse responses as weighted sums of geometric fundamental modes and yield equivalent cascade or parallel realizations. [Session 3, slides 13–23]

DT poles are the roots of the denominator after substituting R→1/z. Real poles control monotone or alternating geometric growth; complex-conjugate poles re^{±jΩ} produce real damped or growing oscillations whose envelope is r^n and angular frequency is Ω. [Session 3, slides 9–27 and 39–44]

The Fibonacci recurrence has poles φ=(1+√5)/2 and −1/φ; its impulse response is a weighted sum of the divergent φ^n mode and alternating decaying (−1/φ)^n mode, giving a nonrecursive closed form for Fibonacci numbers. [Session 3, slides 28–38]

For CT systems, the operator A integrates from −∞ to the present: Y=AX means y(t)=∫_{−∞}^t x(τ)dτ. Replacing DT delays by CT integrators creates a parallel operator calculus for linear constant-coefficient differential equations. [Session 4, slides 2–10]

The CT impulse δ(t) is introduced as the limit of unit-area pulses whose width tends to zero. It is nonzero only at zero yet integrates to one, and its integral is the unit step u(t). [Session 4, slides 14–18]

The one-integrator feedback system ẏ=x+py has system functional A/(1−pA) and impulse response e^{pt}u(t). Each loop traversal adds an integration, building the exponential Taylor series; CT convergence requires Re(p)<0. [Session 4, slides 20–35]

The undamped mass–spring system has conjugate poles s=±j√(K/M). Real inputs excite conjugate mode pairs whose imaginary parts cancel; its impulse response is ω0 sin(ω0t)u(t), with ω0=√(K/M). [Session 4, slides 41–48]

The bilateral Z transform is X(z)=Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞}x[n]z^{−n}. The transform is not fully specified by its rational expression: its region of convergence is essential and encodes whether pole contributions are right-sided or left-sided. [Session 5, slides 14–21 and 25–42]

A right-sided α^n u[n] and the corresponding left-sided −α^n u[−1−n] both have rational form z/(z−α), but their ROCs are |z|>|α| and |z|<|α| respectively. Multiple poles partition the z-plane into candidate annular ROCs. [Session 5, slides 25–38]

For a linear constant-coefficient difference equation, taking Z transforms and using x[n−1]↔z^{−1}X(z) converts the recurrence into algebra; H(z)=Y(z)/X(z) is a ratio of polynomials whose numerator and denominator roots are zeros and poles. [Session 5, slides 22–25 and 43]

Core Z-transform properties in this shard are linearity, delay, multiplication by n (nx[n]↔−z dX/dz), and convolution (x1*x2↔X1X2), with ROCs at least as large as the stated intersections subject to cancellation. [Session 5, slides 22–23 and 44–50]

For a rational DT LTI system, causality corresponds to a right-sided impulse response and an ROC outside the outermost pole; stability requires the ROC to include the unit circle. A causal rational system is stable when all uncancelled poles lie inside the unit circle. [Problem Set 3, Problem 5 and solution]

The bilateral Laplace transform X(s)=∫_{−∞}^{∞}x(t)e^{−st}dt maps CT signals to functions of complex s. Right-sided signals have right-half-plane ROCs, left-sided signals have left-half-plane ROCs, and two-sided signals can have a vertical-strip ROC. [Session 6, slides 7–24]

The same rational Laplace expression can describe distinct left-, right-, or two-sided time functions depending on ROC. For example, e^{−|t|} transforms to 2/(1−s²) only on −1<Re(s)<1. [Session 6, slides 12–24]

Under the bilateral transform, d x(t)/dt↔sX(s) when boundary terms vanish, and δ(t)↔1 by the sifting property. Linear constant-coefficient differential equations therefore become algebraic equations without separately constructing homogeneous and particular solutions. [Session 6, slides 25–33]

Core Laplace properties in the shard are linearity, delay, multiplication by t, exponential weighting, time differentiation/integration, and convolution. The convolution integral maps to the product X1(s)X2(s). [Session 6, slide 34]

For a right-sided signal with no impulse or higher singularity at zero, the initial-value theorem gives x(0+)=lim_{s→∞}sX(s). If the signal has a finite asymptotic limit, the final-value theorem gives x(∞)=lim_{s→0}sX(s); the limit/existence conditions matter. [Session 6, slides 35–36; Problem Set 4, Problem 4]

Forward Euler replaces an integrator by TR/(1−R), producing the pole map z=1+sT. It preserves CT stability only for poles inside the circle of radius 1/T centered at −1/T; for the leaky tank, stability requires T/τ<2. [Session 7, slides 9–20]

Backward Euler replaces an integrator by T/(1−R), producing z=1/(1−sT). It maps the entire open left half of the s-plane into the z-plane disk of radius 1/2 centered at 1/2, so every stable CT pole remains stable after discretization. [Session 7, slides 21–31]

The trapezoidal rule gives A→(T/2)(z+1)/(z−1), or z=(1+sT/2)/(1−sT/2). It maps the left half-plane inside the unit circle and maps the jω axis exactly onto the unit circle, avoiding artificial growth or decay of undamped modes. [Session 7, slides 32–38]

Linearity means weighted input sums produce the same weighted output sums; time invariance means shifting the input shifts the output by the same amount. Together they let any signal be decomposed into weighted shifted impulses whose responses superpose. [Session 8, slides 15–21]

For a DT LTI system, the impulse response h[n] completely determines the system and y[n]=(x*h)[n]=Σ_k x[k]h[n−k]. Convolution acts on whole signals, despite the conventional shorthand x[n]*h[n]. [Session 8, slides 21–42]
The CT counterpart is y(t)=(x*h)(t)=∫_{−∞}^{∞}x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ, obtained by taking the limit of a weighted train of narrow pulses. [Session 8, slides 43–48]

Optical blurring can be modeled as convolution with a point-spread function: a microscope’s three-dimensional impulse response directly measures blur across and along its optical axis, while a ground telescope combines atmospheric and diffraction point-spread functions. [Session 8, slides 50–65]

Repeated poles generate polynomial-weighted modes rather than ordinary weighted sums of distinct geometrics: a double pole at z=1 yields h[n]=(n+1)u[n] and can be realized as two cascaded accumulators. [Problem Set 2, Problem 7 and solution]

Substituting every delay R by R^m maps each original pole to all mth roots of that pole. Substituting R/2 instead halves pole locations; roots of poles inside the unit circle remain inside, preserving stability under the delay-expansion construction. [Problem Set 3, Problem 7 and solution]

The impedance method is exactly the Laplace transform of circuit laws: KCL, KVL, and resistor relations retain their algebraic form, while inductors and capacitors acquire impedances sL and 1/(sC). [Problem Set 4, Problem 6 and solution]

The Fall 2011 Quiz 1 checks that the first seven sessions can be traversed in both directions: waveform→recurrence coefficients, impulse-response shape→poles/zeros, time signal→Laplace transform and ROC, and coupled ODEs→partial-fraction system function. [Quiz 1, Problems 1–4]

Lecture 9, slides 13-17: a signal is an eigenfunction when the system output is a scalar multiple of it; every eternal complex exponential exp(st) is an eigenfunction of an LTI system, with eigenvalue H(s).

Lecture 9, slides 22-25: for a real LTI system H(-jomega)=H*(jomega), so input cos(omega0 t) produces |H(jomega0)| cos(omega0 t + angle H(jomega0)); frequency response is H(s) restricted to the j-omega axis.

Lecture 9, slides 19-21: for a rational H(s), magnitude at s0 is the gain times the product of distances from s0 to zeros divided by the product of distances to poles; phase is the gain angle plus zero-vector angles minus pole-vector angles.

Lecture 9, slides 57-61: for conjugate poles at -sigma +/- j omega_d, the resonant-frequency maximum occurs below omega_d, at omega^2=omega_d^2-sigma^2=omega_0^2-2sigma^2 when that quantity is positive.

Lecture 9, slides 62-67: the mass-spring-dashpot response has phase -pi/2 at the undamped natural frequency omega0=sqrt(K/M), even though its amplitude peak occurs at a lower frequency when damping is present.
Lecture 10, slides 18-24: wallFinder without sensor delay has closed-loop pole p0=1+KT; -1<KT<0 gives monotone convergence, -2<KT<-1 gives alternating convergence, and KT<-2 diverges.
Lecture 10, slides 22-29: KT=-1 puts the sole no-delay closed-loop pole at zero, giving a one-sample response and exact one-step arrival in the idealized robot model.

Lecture 10, slides 36-43: one sample of sensor delay changes the characteristic polynomial to z^2-z-KT and the poles to 1/2 +/- sqrt(1/4+KT); sufficiently negative gain creates complex poles and oscillation.

Lecture 10, slides 48-53: the fastest one-delay response occurs at the repeated pole z=1/2 when KT=-1/4; adding a second delay moves the fastest repeated pole to about 0.682, showing quantitatively that delay slows the best achievable control response.

Lecture 11, slides 15-31: factor a rational transfer function into pole/zero sections; on logarithmic coordinates, products of magnitude become sums, and phase contributions also add, which makes a Bode plot a section-by-section construction.

Lecture 11, slides 8-25 and 33-38: a first-order zero contributes a +20 dB/decade high-frequency slope and approaches +pi/2 phase; a first-order pole contributes -20 dB/decade and approaches -pi/2, with the break at the pole/zero magnitude.
Lecture 11, slides 33-38: magnitude in decibels is 20 log10 |H(jomega)|; the straight-line first-order approximation is exact asymptotically and misses by about 3 dB at the break frequency.

Lecture 11, slides 43-63: for the normalized high-Q second-order system, peak magnitude grows approximately as Q, normalized 3 dB bandwidth shrinks approximately as 1/Q, and phase changes by roughly pi/2 across that bandwidth.
Lecture 12, slides 6-14: the LM741 is modeled as K(s)=alpha K0/(s+alpha) with K0=2x10^5 and alpha=40 rad/s, giving a dominant-pole time constant of 1/40 s and a corner near 6.4 Hz.

Lecture 12, slides 13-23: negative feedback with factor beta changes the op-amp pole to -alpha(1+beta K0), shortens response time and widens bandwidth by 1+beta K0, but reduces DC gain to K0/(1+beta K0); feedback trades gain for speed/bandwidth rather than increasing the initial slew rate.

Lecture 12, slides 25-31: treating DC-motor angle as the integral of voltage, proportional position feedback yields a first-order closed-loop pole at -alpha beta gamma and a step response with final value 1/beta; increasing amplifier gain speeds this idealized model.

Lecture 12, slides 32-39: when motor inertia adds a lag pole, increasing proportional gain makes two real poles collide at -p/2 and then become a complex pair; convergence cannot be made arbitrarily fast by gain alone.
Lecture 13, slides 4-8: the uncertain power-amplifier loop has gain KF0/(1+beta KF0), which approaches 1/beta for large K and becomes nearly independent of both K and the varying plant factor F0.

Lecture 13, slides 9-17: high loop gain reduces the waveform error created by a push-pull transistor dead zone, so negative feedback can suppress a rapidly varying nonlinear distortion, not just static parameter error.

Lecture 13, slides 19-34: the linearized magnetic-levitation plant has poles +/-sqrt(K/M), including one right-half-plane pole; proportional current feedback can move them to the imaginary axis but leaves marginal stability.

Lecture 13, slide 35: adding a zero to the magnetic-levitation controller supplies the extra phase/damping needed to move the poles into the left half-plane and stabilize the plant for sufficient gain.
Lecture 13, slides 36-39: the linearized inverted pendulum has poles at +/-sqrt(g/l), hence one unstable natural mode, but cart-motion feedback can stabilize it.

Problem Set 5 Solution, Problems 1-2, pp. 1-6: convolving with a unit step computes a running sum in DT or running integral in CT; convolving identical exponential modes creates an additional n or t factor, reflecting a repeated pole.

Quiz 2 Solution, Problem 1, p. 2: the two-sided impulse response exp(-|t|) has H(s)=2/(1-s^2), hence the LTI relation y(t)-y''(t)=2x(t); the example tests bilateral-transform reasoning rather than causal assumptions.
Quiz 2 Solution, Problem 4, p. 6: closing gain-4 negative feedback around g(t)=(1+t)u(t) converts G(s)=(s+1)/s^2 into H(s)=(s+1)/(s+2)^2, producing one zero at -1 and a repeated pole at -2.

A CT signal with period T can be synthesized as x(t)=Σ_k a_k e^{j2πkt/T}; orthogonality gives the analysis coefficients a_k=(1/T)∫_T x(t)e^{−j2πkt/T}dt. The complex conjugate in the inner product is what sifts out one harmonic. [Sessions 14–15, slides 16–31 and 3–10]

Only periodic signals can be assembled from harmonics sharing one fundamental frequency. Fourier representation separates waveform shape into harmonic amplitudes and phases, making musical timbre and filtering visible in a common language. [Session 14, slides 3–15]

The unit square wave has a_k=1/(jπk) for odd k and zero for even k, while the corresponding triangle-wave coefficients are −1/(2π²k²) for odd k and zero for even k. A jump produces 1/k decay; one additional degree of smoothness produces 1/k² decay. [Session 14, slides 28–39]

Differentiation multiplies the kth CTFS coefficient by j(2π/T)k; integration therefore divides nonzero harmonics by that factor and requires the DC term to be handled separately. [Session 14, slides 34–38; Problem Set 8, Problem 1 and solution]

Near a jump, ordinary Fourier partial sums retain an approximately 9% limiting overshoot even as more terms narrow the ringing region. Averaging the first N partial sums removes the overshoot in the assigned sawtooth experiment and yields much smoother convergence. [Session 14, slides 39–41; Problem Set 8, Problem 5 and solution]

Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of an LTI system: each input harmonic is multiplied by H(jkω0). An LTI filter changes only the amplitude and phase of existing harmonics and cannot create new frequencies absent from the input. [Session 14, slides 42–50]

A Fourier coefficient is an orthogonal projection under ⟨a,b⟩=(1/T)∫_T a*(t)b(t)dt, directly analogous to resolving a spatial vector into perpendicular coordinate components. [Session 15, slides 3–10]

The speech-production model factors a quasi-periodic glottal source from the vocal-tract filter. Vowels with similar pitch differ primarily through formant resonances; as sung pitch rises, sparse source harmonics sample those resonances less reliably and vowel identity weakens. [Session 15, slides 11–35]

Letting the period T of a periodic extension tend to infinity sends harmonic spacing ω0=2π/T to zero and converts the CTFS synthesis sum into an integral. The resulting pair is X(jω)=∫_{−∞}^{∞}x(t)e^{−jωt}dt and x(t)=(1/2π)∫_{−∞}^{∞}X(jω)e^{jωt}dω. [Session 16, slides 3–15]

If the bilateral Laplace ROC includes the jω axis, the CT Fourier transform is the Laplace transform evaluated at s=jω. The Fourier transform may exist when no Laplace ROC exists, as for a constant or eternal sinusoid represented by impulses in frequency. [Session 16, slides 16–19 and 32–36]

The CTFT inherits linearity, time shift, time scaling, differentiation, multiplication by t, and convolution properties from the Laplace transform. In particular, x(at)↔|a|^{−1}X(jω/a), so stretching in time compresses frequency while preserving spectral area. [Session 16, slides 20–29]
Transform values encode moments: X(0)=∫x(t)dt, and x(0)=(1/2π)∫X(jω)dω when inversion applies. These provide quick normalization checks for proposed transform pairs. [Session 16, slides 27–29]

Duality states that f(t)↔g(ω) implies g(t)↔2πf(−ω). It links a rectangular spectrum to a sinc in time and yields 1/(1+t²)↔πe^{−|ω|} from e^{−|t|}↔2/(1+ω²). [Session 16, slides 30–34; Problem Set 10, Problem 4 and solution]

Canonical generalized-function pairs include δ(t)↔1, 1↔2πδ(ω), δ(t−T)↔e^{−jωT}, and e^{−jω0t}↔2πδ(ω+ω0). A CT periodic signal has a Fourier transform consisting of impulses of area 2πa_k at its harmonic frequencies. [Session 16, slides 32–39; Session 19, slides 6–8]

For a rational DT system, pole–zero vectors evaluated at z=e^{jΩ} give the frequency response magnitude as a product of vector lengths and phase as the signed sum of vector angles. CT evaluates H(s) on the imaginary axis; DT evaluates H(z) on the unit circle. [Session 17, slides 10–28]
For real h[n], H(e^{−jΩ})=H*(e^{jΩ}). Consequently an eternal cosine at Ω emerges with amplitude |H(e^{jΩ})| and phase shift ∠H(e^{jΩ}). [Session 17, slides 14–17]

DT frequency is periodic modulo 2π because e^{j(Ω+2πk)n}=e^{jΩn}. Real cosine frequencies fold about π, so π is the highest distinct DT angular frequency and sampling can reverse intuitive CT frequency order. [Session 17, slides 29–42]

A DT signal periodic in N has exactly N distinct harmonic exponentials, the Nth roots of unity. Its DTFS pair is a_k=(1/N)Σ_{n∈⟨N⟩}x[n]e^{−jk2πn/N} and x[n]=Σ_{k∈⟨N⟩}a_ke^{jk2πn/N}; both x[n] and a_k are periodic in N. [Session 17, slides 45–53]

The DTFS analysis and synthesis matrices are scaled conjugates and inverses. Direct evaluation requires order N² multiplications, which motivates exploiting repeated roots of unity. [Sessions 17–18, slides 48–53 and 17–20]

A radix-2 FFT splits an N-point transform into transforms of the even and odd indexed samples, then combines them with twiddle factors. The recurrence M(N)=2M(N/2)+N gives M(N)=N log₂N multiplications rather than N². [Session 18, slides 19–32]

An aperiodic DT signal is the limit of periodic extensions as N→∞. The DTFT pair is X(e^{jΩ})=Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞}x[n]e^{−jΩn} and x[n]=(1/2π)∫ over any 2π interval X(e^{jΩ})e^{jΩn}dΩ. [Session 18, slides 33–38]

If a sequence's Z-transform ROC contains the unit circle, its DTFT equals X(z) evaluated at z=e^{jΩ}. The DTFT inherits linearity, time shift, multiplication by n, and convolution properties from the Z transform. [Session 18, slides 39–40]

An all-pass system can have unit magnitude at every frequency while substantially altering phase. For H(z)=(1−az)/(z−a), numerator and denominator become conjugate-length vectors on the unit circle, hence |H(e^{jΩ})|=1. [Session 18, slides 5–7]

Time reversal x[−n] maps DTFS coefficients a_k to a_{−k}; for real x[n], conjugate symmetry makes this equivalent to negating every spectral phase while preserving magnitude. Speech played backward demonstrates that phase carries temporal organization. [Session 18, slides 8–14]

In two-dimensional Fourier reconstruction, retaining phase while changing magnitude preserves recognizable object geometry far more strongly than retaining magnitude with uniform or unrelated phase. [Session 18, slides 41–47]

Parseval's CTFS identity is (1/T)∫_T|x(t)|²dt=Σ_k|a_k|². It follows by taking the zero coefficient of |x(t)|² and turns a lowpass cutoff choice into a sum of retained harmonic energies. [Problem Set 9, Problem 4 and solution]

For a periodic extension z(t)=Σ_kx(t+kT), convolution with a time-domain impulse train multiplies X(jω) by a frequency-domain impulse train. Periodic extension therefore samples the continuous spectrum; each spectral impulse has area 2π times its Fourier-series coefficient. [Session 19, slides 9–21]

Sampling x(t) every T seconds can be represented by multiplication with an impulse train. Frequency-domain convolution then repeats scaled copies of X(jω) every 2π/T, producing a periodic spectrum and exposing the mechanism behind aliasing. [Session 19, slides 25–33]

The CT transform of the impulse-sampled signal and the DTFT of its sample sequence have the same shape under Ω=ωT. Thus continuous frequency measured in rad/s maps to dimensionless discrete frequency modulo 2π. [Session 19, slides 30–33]

Periodic extension of a DT signal samples its already periodic DTFT, yielding a representation discrete and periodic in both time and frequency; the impulse weights are again 2π times the DTFS coefficients. [Session 19, slides 34–41]

The four representations form one structural table: periodicity in time implies discreteness in frequency, discreteness in time implies periodicity in frequency, and taking the period to infinity changes a series into a transform. [Session 19, slides 3–9 and 38–42]

A periodic LTI input/output pair is impossible if the proposed output has a nonzero harmonic where the input coefficient is zero, because filtering only multiplies corresponding coefficients. The reverse implication is only permissive: shared support means the pair could be LTI, not that it must be. [Problem Set 8, Problem 4 and solution]

Magnitude-only RC-like filtering attenuates upper square-wave harmonics symmetrically, while phase-only RC-like filtering preserves their sizes but shifts them toward peak alignment and can create a much larger overshoot. Magnitude controls harmonic strength; phase controls temporal alignment and asymmetry. [Problem Set 9, Problem 5 and solution]

For the ideal periodic DT lowpass H(e^{jΩ})=1 on |Ω|<π/2 and zero elsewhere, inverse transformation gives h[0]=1/2 and h[n]=sin(πn/2)/(πn) for n≠0. Applied to a period-3 impulse train, only its DC Fourier-series term passes, so y[n]=1/3. [Quiz 3, Problems 3–4 and solution]

For an echo h(t)=δ(t−T1)+fδ(t−T2), H(jω)=e^{−jωT1}[1+fe^{−jω(T2−T1)}]. Magnitude ripple spacing identifies T2−T1, ripple depth identifies f, and the average phase slope identifies T1. [Quiz 3, Problem 5 and solution]
Lecture 20, slides 2-3: an LTI system cannot create frequency components absent from its input; it can only change their magnitudes and phases, which makes frequency-domain filtering possible.

Lecture 20, slides 12-19: the measured ECG spectrum separates low-frequency baseline drift, the cardiac band, high-frequency noise, and a narrow 60 Hz line; useful recovery therefore combines highpass, lowpass, and notch behavior rather than one cutoff.

Lecture 20, slides 21-28: for a grating of spacing D, constructive diffraction satisfies D sin(theta)=n lambda; first order gives sin(theta)=lambda/D, so far-field spot geometry can estimate microscopic CD/DVD track spacing.

Lecture 20, slides 29-36: under a small-angle approximation, the angular diffraction pattern samples the Fourier transform of spatial structure with spatial frequency proportional to theta/lambda; an impulse train in space transforms to an impulse train in spatial frequency.
Lecture 20, slides 37-43: Fourier features in Franklin and Gosling's DNA diffraction image encode different repeat distances, while the crossed orientation provides evidence of helical structure.
Lecture 21, slides 14-22: impulse sampling writes xp(t)=sum_n x(nT) delta(t-nT)=x(t)p(t); multiplication by the period-T impulse train replicates X(jomega) every omega_s=2pi/T, with scale 1/T.

Lecture 21, slides 19-22: the DTFT of x[n]=x(nT) is related to the impulse-reconstruction transform by Xp(jomega)=X(exp(jOmega)) evaluated at Omega=omega T, exposing DTFT periodicity as replicated CT spectra.
Lecture 21, slides 23-29: if X(jomega)=0 for |omega|>omega_m and omega_s>2omega_m, ideal lowpass filtering separates the copies and gain T restores the original; 2omega_m is the Nyquist rate.

Lecture 21, slides 30-39: aliases are frequency components shifted by integer multiples of the sample frequency into the reconstruction band; once overlapping components have been sampled, their original identities cannot be recovered.
Lecture 21, slides 40-47: an analog anti-aliasing filter must precede the sampler, because digital filtering after sampling cannot undo spectral overlap.

Lecture 22, slides 22-26: resolving a 1,000,000-to-1 amplitude range needs 20 bits because 2^20=1,048,576; raw stereo CD audio requires about 6.3 Gbit, or 0.78 GB, for 74 minutes at 44.1 ksample/s and 16 bits/sample.

Lecture 22, slides 35-49: adding random noise uniformly spanning about one quantization step before quantization converts coherent contouring into noise and preserves local average intensity; Robert's subtractive variant computes Q(x+n)-n when the same noise is available at reconstruction.

Lecture 22, slides 50-60: downsampling by N keeps every Nth sample only after periodic selection, widens the DT-frequency representation by N, and requires prefiltering to prevent overlap; upsampling inserts N-1 zeros and then lowpass filters the spectral images.

Lecture 22, slides 65-75: JPEG's 8-point DCT is equivalent to Fourier analysis of an even, mirrored, period-16 extension; avoiding the boundary jump concentrates energy in fewer low-frequency coefficients.

Lecture 22, slides 76-82: JPEG quantizes high spatial frequencies more coarsely because visual sensitivity is lower there; runs of zero high-frequency coefficients then compress effectively with run-length/Huffman coding.

Lecture 23, slides 3-10: direct radiation of 200-3000 Hz speech would require antennas on the order of 100-1500 km, whereas a 10 cm antenna corresponds to roughly 3 GHz; modulation matches message spectra to practical wireless carriers.

Lecture 23, slides 13-18: y(t)=x(t)cos(omega_c t) creates half-scale spectral copies centered at plus/minus omega_c; multiplying again by the synchronized carrier gives x(t)[1+cos(2omega_c t)]/2, so lowpass filtering recovers x(t)/2.
Lecture 23, slides 19-23: frequency-division multiplexing works when modulated channel bands do not overlap; the receiver translates the chosen band to baseband and rejects the others.

Lecture 23, slides 25-31: a coherent-receiver phase error phi scales the recovered message by cos(phi), vanishing at pi/2 and fading when phi varies; transmitting a large carrier enables simple envelope detection but wastes carrier power and cannot separate summed senders.
Lecture 23, slides 29-30: because speech peak-to-rms ratio can exceed 35, the carrier offset required for envelope detection can consume about 35^2, approximately 1000 times, the message power.

Lecture 23, slides 33-39: digitizing the entire 540-1600 kHz AM band requires T no larger than about 0.3 microseconds; an ideal DT bandpass can be realized by modulation into lowpass filters with in-phase and quadrature branches.
Lecture 24, slide 5: PM uses y(t)=cos(omega_c t+kx(t)); FM uses phase omega_c t+k integral x(t)dt, so its instantaneous frequency is omega_c+kx(t).

Lecture 24, slides 7-8: the small-index FM approximation has the same highest sideband offset as AM; narrowband FM does not achieve arbitrarily narrow bandwidth because integration changes coefficient weighting, not the message's highest frequency.

Lecture 24, slides 9-43: sinusoidal phase modulation produces an increasing number of Fourier-series sidebands as modulation index rises; wideband FM deliberately spends bandwidth on redundancy and gains robustness to additive noise.

Lecture 24, slides 46-60: an ordinary microscope behaves as a spatial lowpass filter; structured phase modulation translates otherwise unresolved spatial frequencies into its passband, making sub-resolution information observable in the experimental output.

Lecture 25, slides 17-34: the CD acquisition chain samples audio at 176.4 kHz after analog anti-aliasing, performs a sharper DT lowpass, and downsamples by four to the stored 44.1 kHz rate; playback reverses this with fourfold upsampling and filtering.

Lecture 25, slides 35-42: pit/land height changes are read interferometrically: reflected optical paths combine constructively or destructively so physical relief becomes an electrical intensity signal.

Lecture 25, slides 43-51 and 63-74: CD focus and radial tracking are closed-loop systems; quadrant combinations A+C-B-D drive focus error, while differential sensor signals steer the track-drive motor.

pedagogy: MIT 6.003 is a representation-first, application-driven signals-and-systems course built around repeated translation among a physical story, differential or difference equation, block diagram/operator functional, impulse response, Laplace or z transform, pole-zero geometry, Fourier representation, and time/frequency response. Concept maps make those translations explicit. Lectures routinely begin from artifacts or systems—leaky tanks, circuits, drug clearance, microscopes and Hubble, a perching UAV, amplifiers and motors, speech, ECGs, radios, images, and the audio CD—then alternate intuition with algebra and graphical reasoning. Short 'Check Yourself' sequences elicit a prediction before revealing a worked answer; staged slides animate recurrences, convolution, pole motion, vector sums, spectral replication, and FFT structure one change at a time. Formal proof is present but secondary to derivation, estimation, transform manipulation, spectral sketching, block-diagram equivalence, and experimentally grounded design judgment. Across 14 problem sets, the course mixes concise exam-style analysis with larger Engineering Design Problems using Python or Matlab, images, circuits, control systems, matched filters, sampling, and communication chains; Sets 4, 7, 10, and 14 are explicitly optional quiz/final practice. Complete solutions show intermediate reasoning, alternate methods, plots, code, and common conceptual distinctions, and the early correction workflow treats self-marking from solutions as part of learning. Three closed-book quizzes and a three-hour, seven-problem final require synthesis rather than formula recall. The progression is deliberate: system representations and transforms; convolution, frequency response, and feedback/control; CT/DT Fourier representations and their relationships; then filtering, sampling, quantization, modulation, and an audio-CD capstone that reconnects analog anti-aliasing, DT rate conversion, optical sensing, and feedback. Prerequisites are calculus, ordinary differential equations, complex arithmetic and Euler's identity, elementary circuits/mechanics, and basic numerical scripting; later sessions assume the transforms, poles/zeros, convolution, Bode plots, stability, and feedback developed earlier in the course.

gems: The opening cell-phone example turns a long acoustic–electrical–radio–optical–radio–acoustic chain into one system block, demonstrating abstraction, modularity, and hierarchy before any transform algebra appears. [Session 1, slides 10–13]

The leaky tank’s time constant is made physical: with equal outlet holes, a wider tank changes height more slowly, and the same conservation equation becomes a capacitor model by replacing accumulated water with charge. [Session 1, slides 25–36]

A difference machine is motivated as compression: store the first large value, then only successive differences when neighboring values are nearly equal. The same idea is immediately shown as words, equation, diagram, and operator. [Session 2, slides 4–22]

The accumulator is the first memorable feedback surprise: one impulse enters, but the output remains one forever—‘persistent response to a transient input’—because every loop traversal writes another sample. [Session 2, slides 37–47]

Fibonacci’s rabbit recurrence becomes a pole calculation: φ and −1/φ reveal one growing and one alternating decaying mode, then combine into a closed form that computes f[n] without f[n−1] or f[n−2]. [Session 3, slides 28–38]

A real six-sample oscillation emerges from poles e^{±jπ/3}; the impulse response 1,1,0,−1,−1,0,… connects recurrence, unit-circle geometry, partial fractions, and periodicity in one compact example. [Session 3, slides 39–42; Problem Set 3, Problem 6]

The CT impulse is introduced through apparently contradictory requirements—nonzero only at one instant but unit total area—resolved by a family of ever narrower unit-area pulses. [Session 4, slides 15–18]

Repeated CT integrations around a feedback loop literally assemble the Taylor series 1+pt+p²t²/2!+…, making e^{pt} a visible consequence of the block diagram rather than a guessed ODE solution. [Session 4, slides 20–35]
One rational Z expression z/(z−7/8) describes either a causal decaying sequence or a noncausal left-sided growing sequence; only the shaded ROC tells which signal was meant. [Session 5, slides 25–33]

The two-sided signal e^{−|t|} produces the vertical-strip ROC −1<Re(s)<1, a particularly clean demonstration that an ROC is the overlap of convergence demands from the two time directions. [Session 6, slides 14–17]

Problem Set 1’s two-tank design goes from conservation laws to a second-order ODE, a cascade interpretation, and a forward-Euler simulation. For T=1 s the one-tank analytic/numerical discrepancy stays below 0.00094 over the tested 60 s. [Problem Set 1, Problem 6 and solution]

The drug-dosing model explains a loading dose with one line of feedback: daily unit doses approach 1/(1−α), so choosing the first dose as 1/(1−α) places the blood level at steady state from day zero. [Problem Set 1, Problem 7 and solution]

An undamped mass–spring is a numerical stress test: forward Euler invents growing oscillations, backward Euler invents damping, and the centered rule closely follows the exact 1−cos t step response. [Problem Set 2, Problem 8 and solution; Session 7]

Approximating a double pole by two nearby simple poles explains both convergence and numerical danger: as ε shrinks from 0.1 to 0.001, two terms of magnitude about 500 cancel to produce values near 1,2,3,… . [Problem Set 2, Problem 7d–e and solution]
The complex-number warm-up j^j=e^{−π/2} is real, because writing j=e^{jπ/2} turns a seemingly exotic power into a decaying exponential. [Problem Set 3, Problem 1a and solution]
The complex geometric-sum design problem turns Σ_{n=0}^{100}(0.8+0.2j)^n into a shrinking spiral and predicts its endpoint near 1/(0.2−0.2j)=(5/√2)e^{jπ/4}. [Problem Set 3, Problem 8 and solution]
A finite triangular pulse is decoded from (1−e^{−s})²/s² as three delayed ramps: +1 slope at t=0, −2 at t=1, and +1 at t=2. [Problem Set 4, Problem 2d and solution]

The impedance-method problem derives a second-order RLC equation by KCL/KVL, then obtains the identical system function by replacing resistor values in an ordinary divider with sL and 1/(sC). [Problem Set 4, Problem 6 and solution]

The microscope resolves a 0.09 μm calibration bead as an approximately 0.53 μm-wide spot and shows still greater blur along the optical axis, making the 3D impulse response an experimentally measurable system signature. [Session 8, slides 58–62]

Hubble’s first star images reveal a mirror ground just 2.2 μm too flat; COSTAR is introduced as ‘eyeglasses for Hubble,’ followed by before/after observations that turn point-spread-function theory into a historical engineering rescue. [Session 8, slides 68–73]
Quiz 1’s impulse-train problem links a CT train of unit impulses at integer times to the geometric series Σe^{−sn}=1/(1−e^{−s}), with ROC Re(s)>0. [Quiz 1, Problem 3b and solution]

A ground/Hubble pair turns convolution into something visible: the broader ground point-spread function smears each point source, while the space telescope reveals much narrower optical blur. [Lecture 9, slides 2-4]

The damped oscillator's amplitude peak is not at either pole's imaginary part or at the undamped natural frequency: the geometry yields omega_peak^2=omega_d^2-sigma^2, while -pi/2 phase occurs at omega0. The live apparatus is simply ten Slinky loops, a bolt, and a motor-driven cam. [Lecture 9, slides 57-67; official transcript 00:12:42-00:14:29]

The perching case starts with a memorable scale disparity: average drag coefficients are 0.16 for a Boeing 747, 0.25 for the Cornell perching plane, and 10 for a common pigeon; matching the pigeon would require a cruising 747 to stop in about 40 meters. The course glider later reaches 1.1. [Lecture 10, slides 5 and 13; official transcript 00:03:38-00:05:23]

The controlled glider enters motion capture at 6 m/s, reaches a perch less than 3.5 m away, and completes the full trajectory in under one second. The guest lecturer adds that an open-loop command misses every time, while feedback hits the perch every time. [Lecture 10, slide 11; official transcript 00:07:12-00:08:27]

The ideal wallFinder reaches a target one meter away in one 0.1-second step by commanding exactly 10 m/s when KT=-1; the pole-at-zero result and physical motion agree perfectly. [Lecture 10, slides 22-29]

One sample of sensor delay changes the fastest possible pole from 0 to a repeated pole at 0.5; one more delay pushes it to about 0.682. The same robot makes delay's cost numerically undeniable. [Lecture 10, slides 50-53]

A first-order Bode magnitude asymptote misses the exact response by only about 3 dB at the corner and rapidly improves away from it, explaining why hand construction is useful rather than merely traditional. [Lecture 11, slide 38]

The high-Q pole geometry yields three compact design heuristics at once: peak gain approximately Q, normalized 3 dB bandwidth approximately 1/Q, and about pi/2 phase change across that narrow band. [Lecture 11, slides 43-63]
The LM741 example uses K0=200,000 but a dominant pole at only 40 rad/s (about 6.4 Hz); feedback converts that apparently poor audio amplifier into a gain-bandwidth lesson. [Lecture 12, slides 6-23]

Op-amp feedback speeds the response and extends bandwidth by 1+beta K0, yet the initial rate of voltage change does not increase—the faster result comes from accepting a smaller final value. [Lecture 12, slides 20-23]

Bach's G-minor violin sonata is played through a transistor crossover-distortion demo at gains 2, 4, 8, and 16, turning an abstract dead zone into an audible experiment; Freeman notes that practical acceptability would require loop gain nearer 1,000. [Lecture 13, slide 17; official transcript 00:17:11-00:19:38]

Magnetic levitation and a spring/mass have nearly identical block diagrams with one sign reversed; that sign rotates poles from the imaginary axis to the real axis and creates an unstable mode. [Lecture 13, slides 26-30]

A threefold zebra enlargement makes convolution's practical payoff visible: pixel replication produces jagged stripes, while the separable triangular filter yields fewer jagged edges. [Problem Set 5 Solution, Engineering Problem 5, pp. 9-12]

The smiley matched filter still finds the nose at column 765, row 432 when Gaussian noise has standard deviation 150—more than half the full black-to-white level difference. [Problem Set 5 Solution, Engineering Problem 6, pp. 13-15]

The suspension design has a counterintuitive bad extreme: with B=100, h(t) is nearly an impulse, so the stiff shock absorber transmits the wheel's bump directly to the passenger compartment and might as well not be there. [Problem Set 6 Solution, Engineering Problem 5, pp. 7-9]

The DTMF detector places poles at the desired 1209 Hz column tone after 10 kHz sampling; r between roughly 0.9 and 0.99 gives discrimination without unacceptable instability or lingering response. [Problem Set 6 Solution, Engineering Problem 6, pp. 9-12]

The same characteristic polynomial has a much wider CT stability range (K>2) than DT (2<K<3), a compact demonstration that 'left half-plane' and 'inside the unit circle' are materially different constraints. [Problem Set 6 Solution, Problems 3-4, pp. 5-6]

Hewlett and Packard's founding phase-shift-oscillator circuit becomes marginally stable at K=8; with 1 kohm and 1 microfarad sections its period is 3.63 ms, and a tenfold resistor change stretches it to 36.3 ms without changing critical gain. [Problem Set 7 Solution, Engineering Problem 3, pp. 5-6]

The robotic-steering design cleanly exposes controller roles: position feedback alone oscillates, derivative feedback alone leaves offset, and the combined controller can converge to the lane center with controlled damping. [Problem Set 7 Solution, Engineering Problem 4, pp. 6-9]

Quiz 2 opens with the noncausal-looking h(t)=exp(-|t|); its bilateral transform gives y-y''=2x, forcing students to separate an LTI input-output equation from a causal realization. [Quiz 2 Solution, Problem 1, p. 2]

The square-versus-triangle comparison compresses a major regularity principle into one picture: the square's 1/k spectrum rings, the once-integrated triangle's 1/k² spectrum converges quickly, and both facts fall out of the differentiation property. [Session 14, slides 32–41]

Fourier's historical provocation is made concrete rather than ceremonial: continuous sinusoids sum to a discontinuous square wave, the very claim Lagrange mocked, and the persistent 9% edge overshoot explains why the paradox remains visible at every finite truncation. [Session 14, slides 18–20 and 39–41]

Instrument spectra turn consonance into arithmetic: notes whose fundamentals share a simple ratio align many harmonic lines, while inharmonic combinations collide without a common low-order pattern. [Session 14, slides 4–15]

The vowel sequence moves from waveform to spectrum to anatomy to singing. One glottal buzz filtered by different vocal-tract resonances explains formants, then high pitch removes enough harmonic samples that a sustained vowel becomes hard to identify. [Session 15, slides 11–35]

The limit from Fourier series to Fourier transform is animated as a sampling-density story: doubling the time period doubles the number of spectral samples in the same band until the line envelope becomes a continuum. [Session 16, slides 3–15]

The ideal lowpass pair is intentionally unsettling: a perfectly rectangular passband in frequency requires a two-sided sinc impulse response extending forever, linking sharp spectral walls to nonlocal time behavior. [Session 16, slides 29–32]

Sampling three CT cosines at T=0.001 s reverses their intuitive order: Ω=3,4,5 fold to effective cosine frequencies 3, about 2.283, and about 1.283 rad/sample, so the 5000-rad/s sinusoid becomes the lowest DT frequency. [Session 17, slides 31–42]

The DTFS has a rare finite-dimensional payoff: N time samples and exactly N roots-of-unity harmonics form inverse matrices, so the abstract series becomes ordinary linear algebra. [Session 17, slides 45–53]

The eight-point FFT derivation counts its own work: direct evaluation costs 64 multiplications, the first even/odd split costs 40, and recursive splitting yields Nlog₂N. The algorithm emerges from reused roots rather than appearing as a black box. [Session 18, slides 19–32]

Backward speech is introduced as a phase-only transformation: real-signal time reversal conjugates the spectrum, preserving every magnitude while negating every phase, yet intelligibility collapses. [Session 18, slides 8–14]

The harbor/mandrill experiment makes phase dominance visceral. Uniform magnitude plus the harbor's phase still exposes cranes and rigging, while the harbor magnitude with uniform phase becomes a nearly unrecognizable texture; swapping spectra follows the phase donor's geometry. [Session 18, slides 41–47]

A single four-quadrant chart unifies all Fourier cases: periodic↔discrete across the diagonal and discrete time↔periodic frequency down the columns, turning four formula sets into consequences of two structural switches. [Session 19, slides 3–9 and 38–42]

Periodic extension and sampling are presented as dual operations with the same impulse-train machinery: repeat in time to sample frequency; sample in time to repeat frequency. [Session 19, slides 9–33]

The sawtooth design problem goes beyond naming Gibbs: students estimate the limiting 1.09 peak and then discover that averaging partial sums removes it, an accessible empirical entrance to Fejér summation. [Problem Set 8, Problem 5 and solution]

The Parseval design problem converts a qualitative lowpass choice into a 90%-energy requirement for geometrically decaying coefficients α^{|k|}, then solves explicitly for the minimum retained harmonic index and cutoff. [Problem Set 9, Problem 4b and solution]

Separating an RC filter into magnitude-only and phase-only thought experiments produces opposite surprises: attenuation removes asymmetry, whereas phase delays without attenuation line up many upper harmonics into a large peak. [Problem Set 9, Problem 5 and solution]
Duality turns a potentially difficult integral into one line: once e^{−|t|}↔2/(1+ω²) is known, 1/(1+t²)↔πe^{−|ω|} follows by exchanging time and frequency. [Problem Set 10, Problem 4 and solution]

Quiz 3 treats an echo as parameter estimation rather than forward calculation: comb-ripple period reveals path-delay difference, ripple depth reveals echo strength f=0.2, and phase slope gives T1=π/1500 before T2=π/300 follows. [Quiz 3, Problem 5 and solution]

A laser and an ordinary CD become a Fourier-transform ruler: with lambda about 500 nm and measured spot angle, the class estimates 1613 nm track spacing against a 1600 nm manufacturing value; the DVD estimate is 704 nm against 740 nm. [Lecture 20, slides 24-28]

The ECG case does not say merely 'filter the noise': its measured spectrum makes learners discover three different contaminants—baseline drift, broadband high-frequency noise, and a 60 Hz line—requiring three complementary filter behaviors. [Lecture 20, slides 12-19]

Franklin's DNA diffraction plate is taught as a two-dimensional Fourier transform: high-frequency bands reveal base-pair periodicity, low-frequency bands reveal a larger repeat, and the diagonal cross signals a helix. [Lecture 20, slides 37-43]

A 0.1 ms-period waveform sampled at 44 kHz makes aliasing arithmetic concrete: its 30 kHz third harmonic reappears at 14 kHz, and subsequent harmonics fold to a surprising sequence of audible tones. [Lecture 21, slides 30-39]

Bach's G-minor violin Presto, performed by Nathan Milstein, is replayed at 44.1, 22, 11, 5.5, and 2.8 kHz, then repeated with anti-aliasing; the lesson makes spectral folding audible before it is merely calculated. [Lecture 21, slides 35-46]

The one-line CD capacity computation—2 channels times 16 bits times 44,100 samples/s times 60 times 74—lands at about 6.3 Gbit or 0.78 GB, linking quantizer precision directly to the physical medium. [Lecture 22, slide 26]

At three bits, direct quantization turns a rose into broad false contours, ordinary dither trades those contours for obvious grain, and subtractive dither keeps smoother shading; one four-panel image makes the noise-versus-bias tradeoff visible. [Lecture 22, slide 43]

JPEG's even period-16 extension is motivated visually: repeating an 8-sample row directly creates a boundary jump and high frequencies, while mirroring it makes the seam continuous and concentrates energy into fewer DCT coefficients. [Lecture 22, slides 68-75]
The final JPEG gallery gives unusually concrete compression anchors: 1% quality is 1666 bytes, 10% is 2550, 20% is 3595, 40% is 5318, 80% is 10,994, and 100% is 47 kB. [Lecture 22, slide 82]

Speech itself is absurdly mismatched to radio hardware: 200-3000 Hz corresponds to wavelengths from roughly 1500 km down to 100 km, whereas a 10 cm phone antenna points toward a 3 GHz carrier. [Lecture 23, slides 3-9]

A pi/2 phase mismatch makes synchronous AM demodulation output exactly zero, and time-varying phase becomes fading; sending the carrier solves synchronization but can spend roughly a thousand times message power for speech. [Lecture 23, slides 25-30]

Wideband FM is presented as deliberate redundancy: increasing modulation index visibly populates many sidebands, spending spectrum so additive noise damages a redundant encoding rather than the sole message amplitude. [Lecture 24, slides 9-44]

The microscopy close turns modulation sideways: the 'carrier shift' happens in spatial frequency, so structure beyond an ordinary microscope's lowpass cutoff is translated into a band the instrument can transmit. [Lecture 24, slides 45-60]

The CD lecture uses a 4x oversampled 176.4 kHz front end to relax the analog anti-aliasing transition, then lets a digital filter do the sharp work before downsampling to 44.1 kHz—the anti-alias lesson becomes a product architecture. [Lecture 25, slides 17-34]

A CD player's focus detector sums opposite quadrants as A+C-B-D, and its track sensor uses a differential pair; a supposedly 'digital' medium closes with two unmistakably analog feedback systems. [Lecture 25, slides 43-51 and 63-74]

Problem Set 11 asks students to reverse-engineer six blurred campus photos. A one-pole guess with p=0.985 and the correct causal/anti-causal row-or-column direction recovers enough detail to name every building. [Problem Set 11 Solution, pp. 1-3]

Problem Set 12 replaces ideal impulse samples with camera-like boxcar integrations, forcing the recognition that a pixel is both a sample and a sinc-shaped aperture filter. [Problem Set 12, Engineering Problem 4 and solution]

Problem Set 13's radio closes a conceptual loop: students identify a 1.25 MHz station from a DT carrier and then decide which analog cutoff, digital cutoff, or sampling changes alter the recovered audio and why. [Problem Set 13 Solution, Problem 5, pp. 8-9]

The final's harmonic-aliasing problem supplies tones at 11, 22, ..., 77 kHz, samples at 40 kHz, and asks learners to label the six survivors below 16 kHz by original harmonic number—a compact test of many-to-one folding. [Final and Solution, Problem 3, p. 4]

The final's 'triple reconstruction' replaces every sparse sample with three area-one-third impulses; the result is not hand-waved as interpolation but derived as multiplication by 1/3+(2/3)cos(omega). [Final Solution, Problem 5, pp. 8-9]
